title: Kneading by hand, the windowpane test
subtitle: How to develop gluten in yeasted doughs without a stand mixer
excerpt: Kneading by hand develops the gluten network that gives yeasted bread its structure and chew. The windowpane test tells you when the dough is ready: a well-kneaded piece stretches thin enough to be translucent without tearing. Most enriched and tin loaf doughs need 8 to 10 minutes of active kneading.
sourceNotes: The windowpane test is a standard gluten-development indicator in bread baking. Hand kneading methods and timing are well-established across conventional bread-making practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A test for gluten development: a small piece of well-kneaded dough stretches thin enough to see light through without tearing. Dough that tears before becoming translucent needs more kneading.

The process by which proteins in flour (glutenin and gliadin) absorb water and form stretchy, elastic chains during mixing and kneading. A strong gluten network traps gas from fermentation and gives bread structure.

content.text: by repeatedly stretching and folding the dough. The physical action aligns the protein chains and builds an elastic network that can hold gas. A tin loaf dough needs 8 to 10 minutes by hand; an enriched dough (brioche, milk bread) needs 12 to 15 minutes because the fat slows gluten development.
Turn the mixed dough onto a clean, unfloured surface. Resist the urge to add flour if the dough feels sticky; it will come together as you knead.
Push the heel of your hand into the dough and away from you, stretching it forward. Fold it back over itself. Give the dough a quarter turn. Repeat.
Work at a steady pace. The dough will feel rough and lumpy for the first 2 to 3 minutes, then gradually smooth. After 5 minutes it should hold together without tearing.

After 8 minutes, pinch off a small piece of dough and hold it between both thumbs and index fingers. Gently stretch it outward in all directions. If it becomes thin enough to see light through without tearing, the
passes and the dough is ready. If it tears immediately, knead for another 2 minutes and test again.
What a well-kneaded dough looks like

Smooth, slightly tacky surface. It springs back slowly when you poke it with a finger. It holds a ball shape without slumping. These are the signs that gluten development is sufficient for a standard tin loaf or roll dough.
A stand mixer fitted with the dough hook achieves the same result in 5 to 7 minutes on medium speed. The windowpane test still applies. Stop and check rather than going on time alone.
